report:
**Conclusion: a qualified “maybe,” not a clear yes.** Hypnosis/hypnotherapy is generally safe and may help some smokers—especially as an add-on to proven treatment—but the best evidence does **not** show it reliably beats counseling, nicotine replacement, or no treatment.

The strongest synthesis is the Cochrane review of hypnotherapy for smoking cessation: across randomized trials, studies did **not** provide reliable evidence of greater long-term quit rates versus other interventions or no treatment, and certainty was low/very low. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235/ Cochrane’s plain-language summary likewise frames the answer as uncertain rather than demonstrably effective. https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking

Individual trials are mixed. A UCSF randomized trial found hypnosis plus nicotine patch was broadly comparable to behavioral counseling plus patch overall, with a possible advantage in people with prior depression—suggesting a subgroup effect, not a universal benefit. https://tobacco.ucsf.edu/research/hypnosis-smoking-cessation-randomized-trial Older claims of ~36% quit rates come from less rigorous meta-analytic evidence with very wide uncertainty and likely methodological/publication bias; guideline evidence reviews note that few hypnosis studies met accepted criteria and there was no clear standardized method to evaluate. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/evidence/ph10-rapid-review-of-nonnhs-treatments-for-smoking-cessation-pdf-392073181532

**Practical takeaway:** don’t rely on hypnosis alone. Use first-line options—behavioral support plus NRT, varenicline, or bupropion—and consider hypnotherapy only as an adjunct from a qualified clinician if it appeals to you.
